Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.
Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
The Southern Armed Forces' statement said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".
It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked the city of Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital, Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the licence fee and use the state budget to fund public media.
Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.
The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.
Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.
Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44; £7.06) a month for public TV and radio.
Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.
"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.
"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."
The protesters say the planned changes could allow politicians to stifle media freedom
Prime Minister Andrej Babis has insisted the government does not want to control public media.
"The funding system is changing, no one wants to control public media, no one wants to dictate to them what they should say and do, no one wants to nationalise them," Babis told the Czech News Agency.
"We are doing this because the system is already outdated and most of Europe is going the same way today and others are joining in," he added.
Some European countries, including France and Norway, have moved away from the public licence fee model in the last few years.
France removed it in 2022 and its public media, which also carries advertising, is now funded by a portion of the income from VAT.
Norway abolished its license fee in 2020 and moved its public broadcaster's funding into the national budget.
Reuters said the proposal would amount to a 15% cut in funding for the public broadcasters Czech TV and Czech Radio.
These protesters held a sign depicting the animated character Vecernicek and saying "We stand with Czech TV"
Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Vecernicek, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.
Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.
Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.
"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.

Türkiye Cumhuriyet Merkez Bankası (TCMB), Birleşmiş Milletler (BM) İklim Değişikliği Çerçeve Sözleşmesi 31. Taraflar Konferansı (COP31) etkinlikleri kapsamında "İklim Değişikliği ve Merkez Bankacılığı: Makroekonomik ve Finansal Perspektifler" başlıklı uluslararası bir konferans düzenledi.
TCMB'den yapılan açıklamaya göre, banka COP31 etkinlikleri kapsamında, 13 Kasım'da Antalya'da "İklim Değişikliği ve Merkez Bankacılığı: Makroekonomik ve Finansal Perspektifler" başlıklı uluslararası bir konferans gerçekleştirdi.
Merkez bankaları, uluslararası kuruluşlar ve TCMB’nin 2021 yılından bu yana üyesi olduğu ve 2026 yılında yönetim komitesinde yer aldığı Finansal Sistemi Yeşillendirme Ağı (NGFS) temsilcilerinin katıldığı konferansın açış konuşmasını TCMB Başkanı Fatih Karahan yaptı.
Daha sonra Hollanda Merkez Bankası ve NGFS Başkanı Olaf Sleijpen bir konuşma gerçekleştirdi.
İklim değişikliğinden kaynaklanan risklerin ve iklim değişikliğinin makroekonomik ve finansal etkilerinin ele alındığı konferansın Mavi Bölge’deki ilk panelinde, TCMB Başkan Yardımcısı Gazi İshak Kara’nın moderatörlüğünde, NGFS’nin ilk ve kurucu başkanı olan Avrupa Merkez Bankası (ECB) İcra Kurulu Üyesi Frank Elderson ve Norveç Merkez Bankası Başkan Yardımcısı Oystein Borsum, iklim değişikliğinin ekonomi, finansal sistem ve merkez bankası politikaları üzerindeki etkilerini değerlendirdi.
Öğleden sonra Yeşil Bölge’de devam eden program, Avrupa İmar ve Kalkınma Bankası (EBRD) Başkan Yardımcısı Mark Bowman’ın konuşmasıyla başladı. Programın devamında TCMB Başkan Yardımcısı Gazi İshak Kara ve banka yetkilileri, önde gelen ulusal ve uluslararası kuruluşların temsilcileriyle birlikte, iklim risklerinin finansal gözetim ve denetim süreçlerine yansımaları ile finansal kuruluşların geçiş planları gibi konularda bilgi ve görüş paylaşımında bulundu.
Konferansın ardından, NGFS ile Türkiye’nin de üyesi olduğu İklim Eylemi için Maliye Bakanları Koalisyonu (CFMCA) tarafından ortaklaşa düzenlenen oturumun açış konuşmasını da Gazi İshak Kara gerçekleştirdi. Kara, iklim değişikliğiyle mücadelede uluslararası işbirliği ve eş güdümün önemini vurguladı.

Hundreds of thousands of Czechs rallied in Prague on Sunday against government plans to replace public media fees with direct state funding, which critics say threatens broadcasters’ independence. Organisers said turnout exceeded a March protest of more than 200,000, potentially making it the largest demonstration since the 1989 Velvet Revolution.
Hundreds of thousands of Czechs rallied in Prague on Sunday against a government plan to cut a public media fee and move funding to the state budget — a policy critics say would dent the broadcasters' independence and viability.
Organisers said Sunday's turnout exceeded an anti-government protest ​of more than ‌200,000 people in March and predicted it could end up as the largest demonstration since ⁠the Velvet Revolution in 1989 that swept away Communist rule and propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.
Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister ‌Viktor Orban, who built an array of pro-government media.
Opposition parties and civic groups also slammed the government for ⁠rushing through the initial bill in the middle of the night in October, calling for the ruling coalition to rescind the law .
"An elected government has the right to govern but it does not have the right to ​do whatever it wants and to dismantle democratic institutions," said Mikulas Minar, chairman of the civic group ‌Milion Chvilek (A Million Moments) that organised Sunday's protest and estimated some 400,000 attended.
"Show that your aim is not to take control of them and let experts propose genuine safeguards for their independence from political power."
Read more Czech author Ondracka: Velvet Revolution an ‘uprising of people who said enough’
The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, ‌backed by the far-right SPD and the eurosceptic Motorists parties, accuses Czech private and public media of bias.
Its draft bill would cancel a 205-crown ($9.26) monthly household broadcasting fee currently ​used for funding. The bill has passed a preliminary vote and awaits further debate.
Protesters, carrying signs that read "Hands off the media" and "Let media deal with politicians", clogged nearby metro stations and filled Letna park overlooking the Czech capital. Speakers included students, soldiers ​and former dissidents who signed the Charter 77 initiative.
Many at the protest, staged days before a public holiday on November 17 ​that commemorates the start of the Velvet Revolution, wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers ​as a tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children 's bedtime stories for decades.
"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," ​pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters. "If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."
Earlier this month, Czech public television and radio workers escalated the fight with a one-day strike that led to broadcast curbs and protests backed by artists and students.
Critics say shifting funding to the state budget would undercut the media's relationship with paying viewers ⁠and make the sector susceptible to political pressure.
A 15% financing cut proposed as part of the change would reduce television's nominal budget to the level of ⁠2008 and that of radio ​to 2005. Media say that is unworkable.
Babis says the government is merely meeting a promise to lighten the financial burden on people.

Independent MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital after an alleged attack last month
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.
In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.
"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.
"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.
"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."
'Targeted' attack on much-loved MP leaves Australian town heartbroken

The independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in Victoria resulting in the amputation of both her legs.
In a statement, Haines said she had moved to the rehabilitation stage of her recovery, which would continue in Melbourne.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred [hospital] and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with Haines.
“We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese said in a statement.
Haines said she was “overwhelmed” by the many Australians who had donated to the Save the Children charity fundraiser.
Her husband, Phil Haines, had made the request to the public on her behalf to donate to the charity in lieu of flowers in the aftermath of the alleged attack.
As of Monday afternoon, more than $1.46m had been raised for the charity through Haines’s fundraising appeal.
“I am overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians in the form of donations to Save the Children and I look forward to working with them in due course on applying these funds to improve the lives of children.”
Haines, the federal member for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was repeatedly struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta on 19 October. Her condition was then downgraded to “serious but stable” on 24 October.
Police will allege the 65-year-old was standing by the boot of her car outside her electoral office when a car did a U-turn and struck her repeatedly.
Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated. He is known to her family.
Police charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Police have also charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, paid tribute to Haines in the Senate on Monday and on behalf of the parliament wished her strength through her challenging rehabilitation.
“It says a great deal about her character that even as she faces these challenges, in her statement she looks ahead to the work she wants to do to improve the lives of children following the donations to Save the Children that Australians made at her request. It is an example of her determination and her generosity that is so admired,” Wong said.
The leader of the opposition in the Senate, Michaelia Cash, added that Haines’s discharge from hospital was warmly welcomed across the parliament.
“She has demonstrated extraordinary courage and resilience. And on behalf, in particular, of my Coalition Senate colleagues, we wish Helen every strength during her continued recovery.”
Haines has been given leave of absence until 26 November, the last sitting day of the year.
MPs across parliament have expressed concern for their safety and that of their staff since the alleged attack, and prompted conversations about the temperature of political debate.
Albanese, during the last parliamentary sitting, warned against the rise in anger “that distorts and corrodes our public discourse”, and urged voters and politicians not to ignore it.
“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials, we are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence.”
The independent MP Allegra Spender said it was “wonderful” news that Haines was making good progress in her recovery.
“She is a remarkable person and her strength and positivity after everything that has happened inspires me.”

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as cracking down on corruption and stronger climate action.

Pontiff delivers forceful speech in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon
Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.
On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.
He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.
In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation .
Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.
During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.
“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.
The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.
Julio Cusurichi, an Indigenous leader, handed Leo a letter during his visit to Pucallpa, asking him to help protect the rights of uncontacted Indigenous relatives.
“The Peruvian state is weakening the mechanisms that should safeguard their territories,” said the letter from the Indigenous rights organisation Aidesep, on which Cusurichi is a board member.
“We cannot allow economic interests to take precedence over the lives and rights of these vulnerable peoples. Therefore, we ask Pope Leo XIV to raise his voice and support this urgent call for their defence.”
Cardinal Pedro Barreto praised the pope’s decision to meet with Indigenous peoples. Barreto, a former Peruvian archbishop who helped win a multimillion-dollar pollution payout for an Andean town, said: “[Leo] is well aware of all the historical suffering … corruption, illegal mining, deforestation, and the contempt shown by politicians.”
Luis E Fernandez, co-founder of Cincia, a scientific research centre in Peru, also hailed the pontiff’s power to raise awareness. “Pope Leo’s recognition of pollution from illegal mining brings much-needed attention to a crisis affecting Indigenous and riverine communities across the Amazon,” he said.
Fernandez visited the Vatican in October and presented Leo with scientific evidence detailing the impact of illegal gold mining and associated mercury poisoning.
Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.
His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.
“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”
The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.
In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip , the longest of his pontificate.

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo pictured in the attorney general's office detention centre in Mexico City in 1989
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
Mexican prison police secured the hospital where Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo was admitted earlier this week
In the 1980s, Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.
Félix Gallardo's life has been portrayed in a number of television programmes including the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The show depicted his rise to power as well as his relationship with Guzmán.

Watch: Prince Harry meets veterans on surprise visit to Lviv
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
Prince Harry watched a wheelchair rugby match taking place inside a noise sports centre as part of his trip
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
Mykhailo Damaskin, pictured with his dog Stitch, has received experimental treatment to walk
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
Prince Harry met Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted by a drone from the front
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Ivan Voinov, who lost a leg, has learned to dance again with his wife
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
A Banksy-style piece of street art in Lviv shows the missiles falling
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

Duke of Sussex meets wounded veterans in city and says country could one day host Invictus Games
Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.
The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine , as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.
It is the British army veteran’s fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.
He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.
He said: “Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.”
Harry watched wheelchair rugby players who hope to be in Ukraine’s team at next year’s Invictus Games , which will take place in Birmingham. Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to the event – its largest ever team.
The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. “When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” he promised.
At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was “still an active serviceman”, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.
Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games”.
The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit , he called Ukraine “a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank” and said “it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that”.
The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo was convicted of the 1985 murder of a US drug enforcement agent and a Mexican pilot.
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80.
Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died at about 2pm (20:00 GMT) on Sunday.
Felix Gallardo, a founder of the Guadalajara cartel, was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent, a crime that made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers.
Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.
Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in the ensuing decades.
Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and a bodyguard for a local governor. Later, he gained a reputation as a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses”.
Felix Gallardo and others set up their cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel.
His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials. His cartel also made innovations, such as using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero.
His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Felix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel.
While already jailed, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar.
Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressured Mexico to arrest those involved.
In 2017, a federal court found Felix Gallardo guilty in the case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings.
His rise and fall were portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series Narcos: Mexico.
Felix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years and was blind in one eye, practically deaf, and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence.
“Thirty-two years have passed,” he said. “That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime.”

Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships in Canada.
It comes despite a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) last month ordering the country's return to the competition.
The hosts then said they would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine.
"Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement.
It added that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer."
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it added.
"The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments."
Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but in October CAS overturned the ban.
It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in five of its events.
The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine, along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships.
Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo.
On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating.
The IIHF's decision was welcomed by the head of Norway's Ice Hockey Federation (NIHF), who claimed the Cas ruling had meant the country would have lost its place to Russia.
"Norway's spot in the World Championship has been restored," said Petter Salsten, Secretary General of the NIHF.
"At the same time, it should be noted that this clarification regarding Russian participation applies only to this specific tournament and is due to the fact that they have been denied entry visas. The situation regarding Russia's participation in other upcoming championships this season remains unresolved."
This is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport.
This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March.
The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.
In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable".
However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria.
While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.
Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.

Pope Leo XIV on Sunday demanded justice for environmental defenders killed while protecting the Amazon and backed Indigenous communities fighting to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging, illegal mining and what he called an “insatiable thirst for domination”.
On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo travelled into the Peruvian rainforest and echoed a central teaching of Pope Francis: that care for the most vulnerable and care for creation cannot be separated.
“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” he told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered on the Ucayali River in Pucallpa, in Peru’s northeast.
He said he had come to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to the 57 murders of environmental defenders that campaign groups estimate took place between 2010 and 2024.
The visit to Cusco, 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues his recovering from lung cancer surgery last month.
Drawing on his years as a bishop in Peru and on Francis’ constant preaching on the environment and Indigenous peoples, Leo used the encounter and a Mass that followed to call for an economic model that respects the Earth and those who protect it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” practised by outsiders.
“Very little has been done — and very slowly at that — while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at Mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
Illegal mining and coca production are also driving deforestation and encroaching on Indigenous territories, putting ancestral lands at risk and exposing communities to violence and organised crime.
On Saturday, Peruvian police reported three operations against illegal mining in Madre de Dios, one of the country’s most biodiverse regions, destroying equipment, rafts and engines valued at €3.8 million ($4.1 million).
In Peru, most killings of environmental defenders go unpunished, and convictions are rare. In 2025, the courts upheld 28-year prison sentences for four timber merchants over the murder of four Indigenous people who opposed logging, after a trial lasting a decade.
The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, ambushed and killed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region in 2023.
In August, a court sentenced four people to up to 35 years in prison. It found Inuma had filed a complaint against the defendants to stop deforestation and other crimes, including drug trafficking, and that they plotted his death because he had spoken out.
Leo also addressed a sharp rise in sexual violence against Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in Condorcanqui province, in the northern Amazon, and condemned the “complicity”, “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding it.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council, Comuawuy, has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the province between January and July alone.
After persistent demands from women’s groups, specialised prosecutors’ offices were created and the government launched a prevention plan. In January, the Ministry of Women and Vulnerable Populations announced a 32-year prison sentence for a man accused of sexually abusing a 14-year-old girl.
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.
In 2025, the Peruvian courts upheld a 28-year prison sentence for four timber merchants for the murder of four Indigenous people who opposed logging, following a trial that lasted a decade.
The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Overall, the 71-year-old has appeared unfazed by the three-nation trip, the longest of his pontificate, which began on 6 November.
While others aboard the papal plane have fallen ill, Leo has shown no sign of fatigue and has seemed energised, particularly by the days spent seeing old friends in his former diocese of Chiclayo.
The Pope mostly sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.

Norway is back in the tournament after earlier being bumped to make room for Russia, following a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling.
Russia will not compete at the World Junior Championship (WJC) following host Canada’s decision to bar Russian players , the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) has said.
The IIHF announcement on Sunday came after the Russian Ice Hockey Federation sought to have next month’s tournament either relocated or cancelled.
Canada took the position in response to a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling late last month that reinstated Russia to international hockey.
Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said on Wednesday that Ottawa opposes Russian and Belarusian participation in international sport “as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity”.
The minister for immigration, refugees and citizenship “will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete, regardless of whether they already hold valid visas”, van Koeverden said.
The tournament features top male players below the age of 20 and is being held in the province of Alberta beginning in late December.
“The IIHF confirms that due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian Government, the Russian U20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship,” the IIHF said in a short statement on social media on Sunday.
“After carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer.”
The CAS ruling overturned the IIHF’s ban, which was imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The IIHF was vociferous in its disagreement over CAS’s decision, and its statement followed announcements from Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic that ⁠⁠⁠⁠their national teams will refuse to play against Russia at next year’s men’s World Championships in Germany.
The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said last weekend that it had been informed that it would be bumped from the tournament to make room for Russia. On Sunday, it said it would now be in the tournament.
“The Canadian government has taken a clear position, and many nations have also taken a stand in recent weeks,” German Ice Hockey Federation CEO Frank H Lutz said.
“We now need that same level of planning security for our home World Championship in May, for the teams, the fans and all our partners. We therefore call on the IIHF to provide clarification soon.”

The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.
Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.
Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.
Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.
Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.
Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."
A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.
Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021 , allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.
Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.
The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.
Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.
Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.
At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

Beijing has a smaller arsenal than Washington and Moscow and worries that any pact could limit its nuclear capabilities.
The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.
Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed.
Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) , which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty.
New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president.
Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party.
New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow.
The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002.
The Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT) from 2003 to 2011, meanwhile, had the same purpose as START I but included less monitoring.
The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended on-site inspections between the two nations in recent years, leaving them dependent on their own intelligence to judge compliance by the other side.
Still, the treaty offered some checks and balances to the two biggest nuclear powers in the world. Together, they possess about 86 percent of all nuclear warheads.
Trump has long wanted China included in the treaty because Washington believes an arms treaty involving only it and Moscow would no longer reflect the global nuclear balance of power.
“Today, the United States faces threats from multiple nuclear powers. In short, a bilateral treaty with only one nuclear power is simply inappropriate in 2026 and going forward,” US Undersecretary of State for Arms Control Thomas DiNanno said in February.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that same month said Trump made it clear that “to have true arms control in the 21st century, it’s impossible to do something that doesn’t include China because of their vast and rapidly growing stockpile”.
Washington also wants a successor treaty to address weapons not covered by New START.
DiNanno has said a new agreement would have to “account [for] all Russian nuclear weapons, both novel and existing strategic systems and [address] the breakout growth of Chinese nuclear weapons stockpiles”.
Beijing’s unwillingness is largely due to the sheer disparity of warheads it currently possesses when compared with the US and Russia.
It has an estimated 620 of them, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), well below the 800 cap each for Russia and the US under New START. Moscow and Washington now have more than 5,000 each, according to SIPRI data. While the US has retired a third of its nuclear warheads so far, Russia has retired less than a fourth.
China’s nuclear arsenal, however, is growing faster than any country’s – by about 100 new warheads a year since 2023, according to SIPRI.
In February, when New Start expired, Chinese officials explained their opposition to joining a nuclear weapons capping agreement.
“China’s nuclear forces are not on the same level as those of the United States and Russia, and China will not participate in disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said in a statement at the time.
This “structural asymmetry” explains China’s reluctance to join a nuclear arms control treaty with the US and Russia alongside its own domestic restraints, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at the Institute of International Studies at China’s Fudan University.
“China maintains a declared no-first-use policy and a ‘minimum deterrence’ posture – nuclear weapons as political instruments for assured retaliation, not warfighting,” Zhao told Al Jazeera.
“From Beijing’s perspective, its arsenal is already restrained by doctrine. The potential US-Russia-China treaty would cap its insurance while imposing intrusive verification on a comparatively small force.”
He also pointed to a “credibility problem”, given the US withdrawal from a number of related treaties, such as the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, which similarly seek to control missile numbers.
In China’s view, Washington has used arms control as a geopolitical instrument, Zhao said.
“Beijing’s strategic logic is that nuclear inferiority invites coercion – conventional or nuclear – while survivable second-strike capability neutralises it,” he said.
China’s smaller arsenal plays a role in its reluctance to join a nuclear arms treaty, but so does its ability to match US capabilities, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
“Chinese assessments also consider US missile defences, precision-strike capabilities and emerging technologies that could weaken its retaliatory capability,” Sun told Al Jazeera.
“An agreement limiting China’s forces while leaving those concerns untouched would have limited appeal.”
According to William Yang, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Northeast Asia, there’s no clear advantage for Beijing and any treaty would be viewed “as a mechanism designed to limit its nuclear modernisation”.
“As a result, Beijing prefers to maintain strategic autonomy in expanding its nuclear arsenal and modernising relevant defence capabilities,” Yang told Al Jazeera.
At the same time, China’s rapid nuclear expansion raises “legitimate questions about where Beijing intends to stop”, said Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong,
“It is difficult to assess China’s ultimate ambitions when it provides little transparency about its nuclear programme. We should not assume that China seeks parity, but neither should we assume that its declared commitment to minimum deterrence fully explains its current build-up,” Reyes told Al Jazeera.
According to the analysts, China would engage in a trilateral framework only when the US and Russia first reduce their arsenals towards “genuine” parity.
It could appear as a “sustained US-China strategic stability dialogue with concrete reciprocity – test moratoria, data exchanges [and] notification of major exercises”, he explained.
The negotiations would also need to address missile defence, advanced conventional weapons and emerging technologies, Sun said.
“Differentiated obligations and phased verification would offer a more workable basis than identical reductions…

The fire is the second blaze in Thailand to cause mass casualties since July.
A fire in ⁠a commercial ⁠building on Thailand’s southern resort island of Phuket has ⁠killed at least 11 people and injured 16 others, according to police.
The blaze in the tourist hub of Patong started at about 3:17am on Monday (20:17 GMT on Sunday) in a building housing a restaurant, rented accommodation and a motorcycle rental shop, and later spread to several other buildings nearby.
Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but an initial investigation found that an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started, ruling out arson.
Phuket Governor Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tyres. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.
Of the 16 people injured, the authorities said, 15 were Thai and one was a Myanmar national, adding that no tourists were among those injured or killed.
The injured were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and injuries from broken glass.
Thailand’s approach to health and safety regulations, especially in bars and nightclubs has long raised concerns.
In July, a crowded bar in the capital, Bangkok, was engulfed in flames and smoke, killing about 40 people after an electrical short circuit triggered the blaze, authorities said.
Four people were killed and many more injured in a fire that swept through a club popular with tourists on Phuket in 2012.
A fire tore through a Bangkok club during New Year celebrations in 2009, killing 67 people and injuring more than 200.

Members of an Arab-led party were reportedly arrested before Israeli elections based on unfounded evidence from the prime minister’s office.
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.
Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government , launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government .
“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election .
Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.
Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.
The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.
The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.
“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.
On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.
Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.
However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

Martine Moise is one of ​33 registered candidates running in Haiti’s first presidential election in a decade.
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 ⁠assassination was ⁠a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.
Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate ⁠on Sunday.
Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs .
“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.
In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.
Martine Moise is one of three ‌women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.
Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.
Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led ⁠Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.
He ⁠was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of ⁠much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.
About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador .
Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.
The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.

Preview of what to expect as President Trump meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China this week.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST: President Trump will meet with some of the world's most powerful leaders this week. China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin and President Trump will be among the attendees to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen China. But while the administration says nuclear proliferation is on the docket, all eyes will be on the U.S.-China relationship. That's now under serious strain after the scandalous departure of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, following revelations regarding a romantic relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Evan Osnos writes for The New Yorker. He has covered China for much of his career and is closely following the APEC summit. Welcome. EVAN OSNOS: Thanks, Rob. SCHMITZ: So let's start with what's been dominating headlines this week, NVIDIA. You know, this scandal is hanging over this upcoming meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping. How do you think this will set the tone? OSNOS: Well, it is a huge development to happen right before a meeting at this altitude of two leaders. I mean, you have now a case that has brought the underlying issues right to the surface, and by that I mean the tension around technology and chips and more specifically, what the Trump administration has set out to do when it comes to allowing or restricting the export of American chips and who it's been listening to. So, you know, Jensen Huang has been one of the president's most trusted voices over the course of the last two years of this administration on technology issues. He is now gone, and so they go into this summit with a scrambled set of inputs. And it's not entirely clear how that's going to play out in the room. SCHMITZ: So I want to pivot to another trade issue here. This week, China extended its trade truce over rare earth exports by two more months to January 10, and for its part, the U.S. is extending tariff exclusions on 178 Chinese products until that date. What is at stake here if these two sides cannot come to an agreement? OSNOS: Well, it's an explosive prospect. But they have managed to avoid having these full tariffs go into effect now for many months, and that's by mutual design. I mean, the - China's economy has weakness on the domestic side. They're still dealing with the outcome of a property collapse, which left 90 million houses unfilled - enough people, by the way, to house the entire population of Russia. They've had youth unemployment - at some points, up above 20%. So they were not eager to get into a trade war. And of course, on the United States' side, Donald Trump's party was just battered in the midterms partly because of the effects of tariffs introduced into trade relationships around the world. So in some ways, he's had reasons to try to hold this off. If, in fact, the truce collapses and they're not able to figure out a way to push this off, this could trigger another round of retaliatory tariffs and a spiral of retaliation that could drive up prices for American consumers. And that comes, obviously, at a moment when voters have signaled pretty loudly that they don't want to see that happen. So the stakes are high for the administration on that score. SCHMITZ: You mentioned the midterms. President Trump took, obviously, a major loss during these midterms, and come January, he's going to be facing a Democrat-controlled Congress. He's only got two years left as president. Is Xi Jinping looking beyond President Trump at this stage? OSNOS: He doesn't have the luxury of being able to write Trump off, but he certainly does come into this meeting knowing that Trump doesn't have a tailwind. Politically, he doesn't have the kind of support in Washington that he could count on if he wanted to try to restart this tariff war. It is, in any diplomatic encounter, sort of job No. 1 - is to understand what your counterpart's vulnerabilities are. That is the thing that you're always asking your intelligence services to give you a briefing on beforehand. And in this case, Xi Jinping comes in with a knowledge of Trump's significant vulnerabilities. But he also knows, and I think this is really important to remember, that from the first term, he got a pretty clear indication that Trump can turn on a dime. And in the latter years of Trump's first administration, when he started to struggle after the midterms and the COVID pandemic came in and began to drag down the economy, he turned his sights on China, started blaming it for the COVID pandemic. He blamed it for his struggles in the 2020 election, and China found itself suddenly in the crosshairs. So I think the Xi Jinping cohort in the Chinese leadership has that memory, and they know that he is somebody you can't quite write off. SCHMITZ: That is Evan Osnos. He's a staff writer for The New Yorker. Evan, thank you. OSNOS: My pleasure. Thanks, Rob.

İstanbul 'da hava durumu 16-21 Kasım haftasında iki kez değişecek. AKOM 'un haftalık tahminine göre salı günü gök gürültülü sağanak etkili olacak, çarşamba gününden itibaren güneyli rüzgâr kuvvetlenip saatte 75 kilometreye kadar çıkacak, cumartesi günü ise sağanak yeniden geri dönecek.
AKOM 'un haftalık tahminine göre İstanbul 'da pazartesi günü hava kısmen bulutlu geçecek, sıcaklık 9 ile 15 derece arasında seyredecek. Asıl değişiklik salı günü geliyor.
Gök gürültülü sağanağın beklendiği salı günü sıcaklık 12 ile 16 derece arasında olacak, metrekareye 10 ila 25 kilogram yağış düşmesi öngörülüyor. Bu miktar, kentte su baskını ve ani sel riskine karşı dikkatli olunmasını gerektiriyor.
Sağanak yalnızca İstanbul'la sınırlı kalmayacak. Meteoroloji'nin haftalık tahmin haritalarına göre yağış salı gününden itibaren Marmara, Akdeniz , İç Anadolu'nun kuzeyi, Karadeniz ve Güneydoğu Anadolu'nun bazı kesimlerinde etkili olacak. Meteoroloji'nin İstanbul için paylaştığı beş günlük yağış takvimine göre salıdan cumartesiye kadar her gün yağış bekleniyor.
Haftanın rüzgârlı kısmı çarşamba günü başlıyor. Güneyden esen rüzgâr bu günden itibaren kuvvetlenecek ve aralıklarla fırtına şiddetine ulaşacak. AKOM , İstanbul ve Marmara'da 15 ile 45 kilometre arasında seyreden rüzgâr hızının hafta ortasından sonra saatte 40 ile 75 kilometreye çıkabileceğini belirtti.
Lodosla birlikte sıcaklık da yükselecek. Çarşamba günü 12 ile 18, perşembe günü 12 ile 19, cuma günü ise 13 ile 20 derece ölçülmesi bekleniyor. Üç günün üçü de kısmen bulutlu ve rüzgârlı geçecek.
İstanbul bu tabloyu yeni tanımıyor. Geçen perşembe ve cuma etkili olan lodos çatıları uçurmuş, ağaçları araçların üzerine devirmiş, Şehir Hatları seferlerinin birçoğunu iptal ettirmişti. O günlerin bilançosu hâlâ akıllarda.
Hafta, cumartesi günü ikinci bir gök gürültülü sağanakla kapanıyor. AKOM 'a göre İstanbul 'da sıcaklık 12 ile 18 derece arasında olacak.
Cumartesi günkü yağış ülke genelinde de geniş bir alanda etkili olacak. Doğu Anadolu'nun kuzeydoğusunda ve Doğu Karadeniz'in yüksek kesimlerinde karla karışık yağmur ve kar görülmesi bekleniyor. Meteoroloji, haftanın en kuvvetli rüzgârlarının hafta ortasından sonra yaşanacağını, hamlelerin saatte 75 kilometreye ulaşabileceğini bildirdi.
İstanbullular için hafta salı günü şemsiyeyle başlıyor, cumartesi günü yine şemsiyeyle bitiyor.

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot said on Sunday caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu must leave office immediately following reports of alleged electoral interference by a Netanyahu aide. The former army chief called Netanyahu and his entourage an immediate threat to democracy, hours after representatives discussed forming a national unity government.
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot on Sunday said caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer", following reports indicating alleged electoral interference by a Netanyahu aide.
A few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government , Eisenkot launched a scathing attack on his rival.
"The behaviour of the outgoing prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his entourage constitutes a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy ," said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Israel 's Channel 12 had earlier reported that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu's chief of staff Ido Norden had phoned in a complaint to the police commissioner's office about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party.
During this exchange, Norden reportedly directed police officers to a purported intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu's office, according to Channel 12.
Read more Netanyahu renews call for Israeli unity government as Eisenkot dismisses 'tricks'
Based on information from this source, three Raam members were arrested. Netanyahu subsequently launched an offensive against the Arab-Israeli parties, accusing them of electoral fraud after they gained a record number of seats.
The three men were later released when the police determined that the information provided by this source was unfounded.
"I call for the immediate opening of an investigation into this affair," Eisenkot said on Sunday, according to a statement from his party.
Netanyahu's office responded by stating that Channel 12's report was "false", maintaining that Norden had "fulfilled his civic duty".
Netanyahu's Likud party accused Eisenkot of "outrageous incitement".
"While the prime minister is extending a hand in the spirit of unity, Eisenkot and his associates issue daily statements filled with venomous, inflammatory attacks," the party said in a statement.
Read more Gadi Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies
The opposition has accused the caretaker premier of seeking to delegitimise Arab parties and the election in an attempt to cling to power.
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's opposition secured the 61 seats required to form a government following last month's election.
The two main Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, have indicated support for Eisenkot, who was tapped to form a government last week.
On Saturday, Netanyahu appealed to Eisenkot to join him in a unity government, but the former army chief accused him of playing "tricks" and sowing tensions.
